title: Four buckets
teaches: Pre-tax, Roth, HSA and taxable accounts compared by the tax rate on the way in and on the way out, why pre-tax often wins for someone with low-income years ahead, and the 2026 limits

blocks.text: A dollar of pay you decide to save can go into one of four kinds of account. It can go into a traditional 401(k) or IRA before tax, into a Roth 401(k) or IRA after tax, into a health savings account, or into an ordinary brokerage account. The investments inside can be identical: the same index fund in all four. What differs is when, and whether, the government takes its share.

**Pre-tax:** no income tax on the way in, and the growth isn't taxed each year, but every dollar that comes out is ordinary income. **Roth:** taxed on the way in, then nothing more, ever, if the rules are followed (broadly, the account has been open five years and you are 59½; lesson 9 covers the exceptions). **HSA:** no tax on the way in or out, if the money is spent on health care. **Taxable:** taxed on the way in, dividends taxed each year, and the gain taxed when you sell, at the rates for gains from lesson 7.
Most advice about which to use is a rule of thumb about age or income. This lesson replaces it with the comparison underneath: the tax rate on the way in against the tax rate on the way out.

Put $10,000 of pay into a pre-tax account at a 5 percent real return for twenty years. It grows to $26,500, and if withdrawals are taxed at 22 percent you spend $20,700. Put the same $10,000 of pay into a Roth instead: 22 percent tax first leaves $7,800 to deposit, which grows to $20,700. Exactly the same. Multiplication doesn't care about order, so if the rate is the same both ways, the two accounts are identical.[^equal]
So the whole question is whether your rate on the way out will be higher or lower than your rate on the way in. Guess first, then try it.

blocks.caption: What $10,000 of pay leaves to spend after some years in each account. The taxable account assumes a 2 percent dividend yield and 15 percent on dividends and the final gain; the HSA assumes the money is spent on health care.
blocks.task: Guess, then set the rates equal, and then try a rate out near zero

blocks.text: The figure has a slider for the number of years too. The years don't change which account wins, only by how much in dollars. As long as the money is spent on health care, the HSA always comes out on top, because it skips tax at both ends. The taxable account trails the Roth by the tax on dividends along the way and on the gain at the end, though for someone whose gains will fall in the 0 percent band, that last part disappears.

parts.title: Why the rate out is often low

blocks.text: The rate in is easy to know: it is your marginal rate, the rate on your last dollars of pay, because those are the dollars a pre-tax contribution keeps off your tax return. For most professional couples it is 22 or 24 percent, plus any state tax.

The rate out is not a marginal rate. Withdrawals fill the tax return from the bottom, through the standard deduction and the 10 and 12 percent brackets, so what matters is the average rate across them. A couple with no other income can take $32,200 out of a pre-tax account tax-free, and $100,000 for $7,640, under 8 percent.

blocks.caption: The average federal rate on a year's pre-tax withdrawals for a married couple with no other income, against the 22 percent saved on each dollar put in.

blocks.text: That gap, 22 or 24 percent saved on the way in and about 5 to 9 percent paid on the way out by a couple withdrawing $60,000 to $130,000 a year, is why pre-tax contributions usually win for anyone who expects years of low income between leaving work and claiming Social Security. It is the gap that lessons 9 and 10 exploit: with years of low income ahead, pre-tax money can be moved into a Roth cheaply, at 10 or 12 percent, before it is needed. That move, paying the income tax now to shift money from a pre-tax account into a Roth, is a **Roth conversion**.

Things that push the rate out up, and favour the Roth: a large pension or Social Security, which fill the low brackets first; **required minimum distributions**, the withdrawals the law forces from pre-tax accounts each year from age 73 (75 for anyone born in 1960 or later), on a large balance (lesson 12); a surviving spouse filing as single, with brackets half as wide; moving to a state with income tax; heirs who will inherit pre-tax money in their own peak earning years. And nobody knows what rates will be in 2050. Some Roth money hedges that, which is why many planners suggest holding some of each.

An HSA is open only to people covered by a high-deductible health plan, including one bought on the marketplace before 65, and not to anyone enrolled in Medicare,[^hdhp] but for them it is the best account the tax code offers. Contributions come off taxable income, and through payroll they also skip the 7.65 percent Social Security and Medicare tax, which even a 401(k) doesn't. The money can be invested, grows untaxed, and comes out untaxed for medical costs.

The useful trick is that there is no deadline for reimbursement. Pay a medical bill from ordinary savings today, keep the receipt, leave the HSA invested, and reimburse yourself from it in twenty years. In effect the account becomes a second Roth, which can be drawn on at any age by matching old receipts.[^receipts]

After 65 an HSA can also be spent on anything, taxed as ordinary income like a traditional IRA, with no penalty. Before 65, money spent on anything other than health care is taxed as income and also charged a 20 percent penalty. The 2026 limits are $4,400 for self-only coverage and $8,750 for a family, plus $1,000 from age 55.

parts.title: Taxable accounts, and what to fill first

blocks.text: A taxable brokerage account looks like the worst of the four, and for a single deposit held thirty years it is. Yet it has three things the others lack. There are no age rules: the money is available at any time, which matters to anyone planning to stop work before 59½ (lesson 9). The **basis**, what you paid for the shares, comes back untaxed, so selling $100,000 of shares bought for $70,000 adds only $30,000 to income. And a couple whose income is mostly long-term gains can sit in the 0 percent band for gains from lesson 7.

The 2026 contribution limits are $24,500 for a 401(k), plus $8,000 from age 50 or $11,250 from 60 to 63; and $7,500 for an IRA, plus $1,100 from 50. From 2026, workers whose wages from the same employer were more than about $150,000 the year before must make their 401(k) catch-up contributions to a Roth.[^catchup] A couple whose income is above about $242,000 in 2026 ($153,000 single) can't put money into a Roth IRA directly, but can usually get there by a side route, the **backdoor Roth**, which the branch on equity pay and high earners explains along with the mega backdoor. In a low-income early-retirement year, the limit doesn't bite.

A common order of filling: take any employer match first, the money an employer adds to your 401(k) when you contribute, since matching 50 cents or a dollar on each of your dollars is an immediate return of 50 or 100 percent; then an HSA if eligible; then the 401(k) and IRA, pre-tax or Roth by the comparison above; and then a taxable account. Someone planning to stop work early may want the taxable account to grow larger than this order would make it, as the next lesson shows.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Pre-tax and Roth come out exactly equal when the tax rate in equals the rate out.
The rate in is your marginal rate; the rate out is the average rate on withdrawals that fill the brackets from the bottom.
Low-income years ahead favour pre-tax contributions; large pensions, required withdrawals and a surviving spouse favour Roth.
An HSA skips tax at both ends and can be reimbursed from at any age with old receipts.

blocks.caption: Six questions on the four buckets
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Someone in the 24 percent bracket expects to pay 24 percent on withdrawals later. Which account leaves more to spend, pre-tax or Roth?
choices: Pre-tax, because the money grows for longer
items.why: With equal rates, both are the same $10,000 of pay times the same growth times one minus the same rate. Only the order differs.

items.ask: Why is the rate on the way out often lower than the rate on the way in?
choices: Withdrawals fill the brackets from the bottom, starting with the standard deduction
Withdrawals are taxed as capital gains
Retirement accounts are taxed at a flat 10 percent
items.why: Contributions save tax at your top rate, but withdrawals in a low-income year are taxed at 0, 10 and 12 percent, averaging far less.

items.ask: A married couple with no other income withdraws $100,000 from a traditional IRA in 2026. About what share goes in federal income tax?
items.why: After the $32,200 deduction, $67,800 is taxed at 10 and 12 percent, $7,640 in all.

items.ask: Which of these favours Roth contributions over pre-tax?
choices: A large pension that will fill the low brackets in retirement
Planning several years of low income before Social Security
Being in the 24 percent bracket while working
items.why: A pension takes up the low brackets, so pre-tax withdrawals land in higher ones, raising the rate out.

items.ask: What can an HSA do that a 401(k) can't?
choices: Avoid Social Security and Medicare tax on contributions made through payroll
Be opened without any health plan
items.why: HSA payroll contributions skip the 7.65 percent payroll tax, and withdrawals for medical costs are never taxed.

items.ask: You sell $100,000 of shares from a taxable account that you bought for $70,000 two years ago. What goes on your return?
choices: Nothing, since the account was funded with taxed money
items.why: The $70,000 basis comes back untaxed; only the gain is income, at the long-term rates.

summary: **Four wrappers, one investment.** Pre-tax, Roth, HSA and taxable can all hold the same fund; only the timing of tax differs.
**Equal rates, equal results.** Pre-tax and Roth come out the same when the rate in matches the rate out.
**The rate in is marginal; the rate out is average.** Withdrawals fill the brackets from the bottom, through the standard deduction.
**Low-income years favour pre-tax.** A couple can take $32,200 a year tax-free and $100,000 for under 8 percent.
**Some things favour Roth.** Pensions, large required withdrawals, a surviving spouse filing single, and state taxes later.
**The HSA beats them all for health costs.** No tax in or out, no payroll tax through work, and reimbursement at any age.
**Taxable accounts give flexibility.** No age rules, the basis back untaxed, and access to the 0 percent band for gains.

equal.title: Why they match
equal.text: Pre-tax: $10,000 × growth × (1 − rate). Roth: $10,000 × (1 − rate) × growth. The same three numbers multiplied in a different order. That holds for the same pay. The limits are a different matter: they count dollars deposited, not pay. A full $24,500 Roth deposit is all after-tax money, while $24,500 pre-tax still owes tax on the way out, so someone who can fill the limit either way shelters more in the Roth.

receipts.title: Keeping receipts
receipts.text: The IRS can ask for proof that a reimbursement matches a qualified medical expense paid after the HSA was opened. A folder of scanned bills and explanations of benefits, kept as long as the account, is enough. The expense must have been paid while the account existed, not before.

catchup.title: Roth catch-ups
catchup.text: The SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 requires catch-up contributions from anyone whose wages from that employer were above a threshold in the previous year, set at $145,000 and raised for inflation, to go into a Roth 401(k). After a delay, the rule applies from 2026. Check the exact threshold for the year.

hdhp.title: High-deductible plans
hdhp.text: To qualify for an HSA in 2026, a health plan must have an annual deductible of at least $1,700 for self-only coverage or $3,400 for a family, and cap annual out-of-pocket costs at $8,500 or $17,000. You also cannot be enrolled in Medicare or covered by another non-qualifying plan.
